body.heading: The body keeps the tension
paragraphs: Long after a stressful moment passes, the body often keeps holding its position: jaw set, shoulders up near the ears, fists half-closed, breath shallow, stomach braced. We stop noticing because the holding becomes the background — until the headache or the aching neck files a complaint.
A body scan sounds formal, but the everyday version is simple: tour the usual hiding places, one at a time, and deliberately let each one soften.

body.heading: A two-minute tour
paragraphs: Start at the top: forehead smooth, jaw unclenched — let your teeth part slightly and your tongue drop from the roof of your mouth. Shoulders: lift them to your ears once, then drop them like a sigh. Hands: open them flat, stretch the fingers, let them rest.

Continue down: soften the stomach instead of bracing it, uncross the ankles, feel the full weight of your feet on the floor. Breathe out slowly as you go. The whole tour takes two minutes and needs no equipment, no privacy and no explanation to anyone nearby.

body.heading: Set traps for tension during the day
paragraphs: Tension rebuilds, so build reminders into the day’s furniture: every time you open a door, drop your shoulders. Every red light or loading screen, unclench the jaw. Attach the check to something that happens twenty times a day and the habit maintains itself.

Persistent pain or tension that does not ease deserves proper attention — a doctor, dentist or physiotherapist depending on where it lives. This tour is for ordinary stress held in ordinary muscles, and for that, it is surprisingly effective.

takeaway: Tour the hiding places — jaw, shoulders, hands, stomach — and let each one stand down.
